nameStory: The 'blunt-tailed snake millipede' gets its name from its rounded, blunt rear end that lacks the pointed tip found on many other millipedes. The 'snake' part comes from its smooth, cylindrical body that moves in serpentine waves as it crawls through leaf litter. Despite the name, it's definitely not a snake — it's a gentle decomposer with dozens of tiny legs!
description: The blunt-tailed snake millipede is a small, worm-like creature that's actually an arthropod related to insects and spiders. It has a smooth, cylindrical body divided into many segments, each bearing two pairs of tiny legs that create a wave-like motion as it moves. These millipedes are typically dark brown to blackish in color and reach about 1-2 inches in length. Originally from Europe, they've established themselves in North American forests where they help break down decaying plant matter.

idTips.label: Blunt tail end
idTips.description: The rear end is distinctly rounded and blunt rather than pointed or tapered — run your finger gently along its length and you'll feel the abrupt, smooth end

idTips.label: Smooth cylindrical body
idTips.description: Body feels smooth to the touch, like a firm piece of cooked spaghetti, without ridges, bumps, or bristles that some millipedes have

idTips.label: Dark coloration
idTips.description: Usually dark brown to nearly black, sometimes with a slight glossy sheen that catches the light when moist

idTips.label: Wave-like movement
idTips.description: Moves in distinctive undulating waves rather than the more rigid movement of some millipedes — watch how the body flows like a tiny snake

idTips.label: Coiling behavior
idTips.description: When disturbed, curls into a loose spiral or coil rather than a tight ball — feels firm but flexible when gently handled

habitat: Look for these millipedes in moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, especially under fallen logs, leaf litter, and decomposing organic matter. They prefer well-drained but consistently damp soil in wooded areas with maple, oak, and birch trees. You'll often find them in gardens and compost piles near forest edges.

seasonality.spring: Active as temperatures warm, often seen crawling on the surface after spring rains. Young individuals may be more numerous and easier to spot.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid periods and after rainfall. During dry spells, burrow deeper into soil and leaf litter, so check under logs and stones.
seasonality.fall: Very active as they feed on freshly fallen leaves. This is often the best time to observe them as they work through the new leaf litter.
seasonality.winter: Move deeper into soil and under thick leaf litter to avoid freezing. Rarely seen on the surface except during warm winter days.

funFact: Despite having 'millipede' in their name (meaning 'thousand feet'), blunt-tailed snake millipedes actually have far fewer legs — typically around 100-200 depending on their age, since they add more body segments and legs each time they molt throughout their lives!
confusionNotes: Often confused with earthworms at first glance, but millipedes have visible legs and segmented bodies while earthworms are smooth and legless. Memory trick: 'Millipedes have many feet, worms are neat and complete' — look for the tiny legs moving in waves along the sides.
contextualKnowledge: This is an introduced species from Europe that has become well-established in North America. While 'millipede' literally means 'thousand feet,' no millipede species actually has that many legs — it's just an old exaggeration that stuck as the common name for the entire group.
compareHints: The blunt-tailed snake millipede is distinguished from its relative Cylindroiulus caeruleocinctus by its distinctly blunt rear end and typically darker coloration. While both species have smooth, cylindrical bodies, the blunt-tailed variety lacks the subtle color bands that may be present on some other barrel millipedes. The blunt tail is the most reliable feature for separating it from other similar millipedes in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Very similar to its relative the Blunt-tailed Snake Millipede, but the Blue-banded species shows those characteristic bluish markings around each segment while the Blunt-tailed tends to be more uniformly dark.
